summary: A description of two new commands in UCSB's Simple-Minded File System: Login (LGI), which identifies the user and an account for billing, and Logout (LGO). Users should issue LGI right after the connection setup. Use was not yet billed, but accounting was requested. It was replaced by RFC 431.

eli5.summary: Two new buttons for a file locker: one to say who you are and who pays, and one to say goodbye.

subtitle: Authentication and accounting for UCSB file access

tldr.problem: UCSB's Simple-Minded File System (SMFS) needed a way to identify users and track which account should be billed for their file operations.
tldr.mechanism: Two new commands were added: Login (LGI, opcode 13) identifies the user and account number that remains in effect until another Login or Logout; Logout (LGO, opcode 14) terminates the current accounting association. Both commands use fixed-length user names (8 characters) and account numbers (4 characters).
tldr.outcome: The accounting commands allowed SMFS to prepare for billing when billing was later enabled, and to collect usage statistics.

today: RFC 399 is historic and was superseded by RFC 431. The SMFS accounting commands were a simple form of authentication and billing tracking for early network file access.

sections.title: Accounting for File Access
sections.content:
RFC 399 describes two new commands added to UCSB's Simple-Minded File System (SMFS): the Login command and the Logout command. These commands allow SMFS to identify users and track which account should be billed for file operations.

At the time of publication, SMFS was not yet billing for use, but the commands were designed to prepare for future billing and to collect usage statistics.
sections.eli5: The file locker needed to know who was using it so it could later bill the right account.

sections.title: Login and Logout Commands
sections.content:
The Login (LGI) command, with opcode 13, identifies the user and specifies the account number. The user should issue Login directly after completing the connection setup (ICP) and before any command referencing a file. The user name and account remain in effect until another Login command is issued, a Logout command is issued, or the connection closes.

The Logout (LGO) command, with opcode 14, terminates the current accounting association without closing the connection. The user must issue another Login before performing file operations after logout.
sections.eli5: When you arrive, you say your name. Everything you do gets billed to your account. When you leave, you say goodbye, but stay connected if you want.

sections.title: Command Format
sections.content:
Login messages contain an 8-bit opcode (13), followed by a user name field and an account number field. Both fields use the same format: an 8-bit length followed by that many 8-bit characters. The maximum user name length is 8 characters; the maximum account number length is 4 characters. Both must use characters from the same character set as filenames.

Logout is simpler: just the 8-bit opcode (14) with no arguments.
sections.eli5: Login says: the number 13, then how many letters your name has, then your name, then how many numbers your account has, then your account. Logout just says the number 14.

references.text: Krilanovich, M., "SMFS Login and Logout," RFC 399, September 1972.
